The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Summary of 2005 Policy Manifesto

This manifesto outlines a comprehensive policy platform centred on environmental sustainability, social equity, and democratic reform.

## Economic Policy

The document advocates for wealth redistribution through progressive taxation, with higher rates on upper incomes and corporate profits. It proposes replacing Value Added Tax with environmental taxes based on resource usage and pollution. A Land Value Tax would replace existing property taxes. The manifesto supports economic localisation through community banks, credit unions, and local currencies, while opposing adoption of a single European currency. It emphasises measuring wellbeing beyond traditional economic indicators.

## Energy and Climate

The manifesto adopts a "Contraction and Convergence" framework for emissions reduction, targeting 20% reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. Policies include a carbon tax, increasing renewable energy to 40% by 2020, implementing energy efficiency programmes, and phasing out nuclear power. A dedicated cabinet position for climate policy coordination is proposed.

## Welfare Reform

Central to the welfare proposals is a universal "Citizen's Income" providing unconditional basic income to all residents, replacing means-tested benefits. A "Citizen's Pension" would provide guaranteed retirement income linked to average earnings, eliminating means-testing. Additional measures include simplified child benefits, reduced working hours, and increased affordable housing through reformed land ownership and local authority investment.

## Public Services

Healthcare policy focuses on returning the health service to founding principles of universal comprehensive care, opposing privatisation and public-private partnerships. The manifesto proposes abolishing prescription charges, restoring free eye and dental care, and increasing funding to European average levels. Education priorities include scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, abolishing standardised testing for younger pupils, and increasing overall funding.

## Transport

Transport policy prioritises public transport, walking, and cycling over private vehicles. Proposals include returning rail and underground networks to public ownership, extending congestion charging, increasing fuel duties, and taxing aviation fuel. The manifesto targets a 10% reduction in road traffic by 2010, redirecting road-building funds to public transport improvements.

## Environment

A "Zero Waste Strategy" would aim for 60% domestic waste recycling by 2010, banning incineration and establishing a dedicated agency for resource recovery. The manifesto applies precautionary principles to new technologies including genetic modification, opposes patents on natural resources, and strengthens animal welfare protections including banning live animal exports.

## Food and Agriculture

Agricultural policy proposes replacing European agricultural subsidies with support for organic farming and local food markets, targeting 30% organic production by 2012. The manifesto opposes genetically modified food and seeks to address anti-competitive behaviour by major retailers.

## Crime and Justice

Crime reduction focuses on community-based prevention, improved urban design, increased community policing, and youth facilities. The manifesto proposes stricter gun control legislation and expanded restorative justice programmes as alternatives to imprisonment.

## Democratic Reform

Constitutional proposals include opposing identity cards, introducing proportional representation for all elections, reforming regional government, establishing an elected upper chamber, and creating a written constitution. The manifesto opposes the proposed European constitutional treaty while supporting continued European engagement.

## International Policy

Foreign policy emphasises peaceful diplomacy, nuclear disarmament, reduced military spending, and increased overseas aid to 1% of national income. The manifesto supports cancelling debts of the poorest countries, reforming international institutions including the United Nations, and replacing current trade organisation rules with agreements prioritising sustainability and local economies over global trade expansion.

# Summary of 2005 General Election Manifesto

## Core Principles

The manifesto is built on three principles: individual freedom with minimal unnecessary government interference, fairness through provision of essential services (education, healthcare, pensions, environment, policing), and trust through democratic accountability and decentralisation of power.

## Healthcare Proposals

Key commitments include free personal care for elderly and disabled people, quicker diagnostic pathways using both public and private facilities, free eye and dental check-ups, expanded prescription charge exemptions, recruitment of additional medical staff, and removal of centralised bureaucratic targets. Prevention initiatives include banning smoking in enclosed public places, school meal nutrition standards, and restricting unhealthy food advertising to children.

## Education and Skills

The manifesto proposes abolishing university tuition fees, cutting infant class sizes to an average of 20 pupils, ensuring core subjects are taught by qualified specialists, and reducing external testing. Other commitments include expanding Children's Centres, reforming school discipline policies, combining academic and vocational qualifications into a diploma system, and maintaining free school transport.

## Economic Approach

Proposals include adhering to fiscal rules limiting government borrowing and debt, giving independent auditing powers to scrutinise budget figures, simplifying business taxation, introducing a 50% tax rate on income above £100,000 annually, abolishing Council Tax in favour of income-based local taxation, cutting stamp duty thresholds, and reducing regulations on businesses.

## Pensions and Benefits

Commitments include guaranteeing increased basic pension from age 75 linked to earnings, introducing a residency-based citizen's pension addressing women's pension inequality, increasing maternity pay, reforming employment support programmes, abolishing the Child Support Agency, providing winter fuel payments to severely disabled people, and improving compensation for workers affected by failed company pension schemes.

## Crime and Justice

Proposals include recruiting 10,000 additional police officers, expanding community support officers, implementing community justice panels for non-violent offenders, using Acceptable Behaviour Contracts, improving prison education and skills training, creating a UK Border Force, opposing identity card schemes, opposing reductions in jury trial rights, and reforming asylum assessment processes.

## Local Communities

Key policies include replacing Council Tax with income-based local taxation, releasing public land for 100,000 affordable homes, freeing councils from central government controls, merging inspection bodies, protecting post office networks, and setting municipal waste reduction targets including 60% household recycling within seven years.

## International Affairs

The manifesto criticises military intervention in Iraq as lacking proper legal authority, commits to working within international institutions, supports UN reform and EU constitutional changes subject to referendum, advocates increasing international aid to 0.7% of national income, and proposes working for fair trade agreements whilst ending agricultural subsidies that harm developing economies.

## Environment

Environmental policies throughout the manifesto include achieving renewable energy targets of 20% by 2020, introducing carbon taxation, not replacing nuclear power stations, implementing vehicle taxation based on emissions, promoting public transport investment, establishing environmental tribunals, and pressing for international climate agreements based on per-capita emissions convergence.

## Governance Reform

Constitutional proposals include curbing prime ministerial powers, requiring parliamentary approval for military action, establishing a predominantly elected second chamber, introducing proportional representation for elections, reducing ministerial numbers, strengthening parliamentary scrutiny, and enhancing devolution to Scotland and Wales.
